texts: 4 September–12 October 2026. We explored how pre-arrival care could help guests feel recognised while keeping the hotel’s promises deliverable.
Sources: S02 assigned brief; 7 & 16 Sep MO interviews; process wall; final presentation.   |   Case study 01/10

We began with a tension in luxury hospitality: asking about a preference creates an expectation. More questions can multiply combinations of room preparation, timing and service requests, while staff capacity, room changes and cost to serve remain constrained. The brief described an earlier hyper-personalisation pilot that had been stopped because of operational complexity.

We were asked to build engagement and manage expectations after booking and before arrival, without over-promising. The commercial intent was brand equity, loyalty and spending on property. This was not a booking-conversion brief.
The brief as we reframed it

We are solving for pre-arrival care that helps guests feel recognised and can be delivered reliably at manageable cost and complexity, in service of Mandarin Oriental’s goal of strengthening brand equity and guests’ willingness to pay.

We chose an urban MO context and a high-net-worth guest segment, often represented by a human assistant. The “top 5%” boundary was our design focus, not a verified segment size. We connected what the assistant knows before arrival with what a Dream Maker may notice in person, then asked how both could become an owned, feasible service response.
Interrogate the brief; separate facts, assumptions and questions; hear Kate’s account.
Build evidence through fieldwork, MO conversations and assistant interviews; challenge the initial framing.
Develop insights, compare concepts, map stakeholders and work through the service journey.
Connect user value to business measures; write criteria and failure conditions.
Iterate the room prototype and Dream Maker workflow; assemble the final proposition and playback.
The timeline follows dated course and project records. Some workshop artefacts are undated; their exact production day is not inferred.
Fig. 1. Our early Facts / Assumptions / Checks wall. The case study follows the work behind the conclusion.
Evidence, access and the voices we missed
We combined proxy expertise, small field samples and assistant accounts. These inputs revealed a service opportunity, but they did not establish a universal communication problem.
Sources: Kate interview 7 Sep; MO interview 16 Sep; final research deck; assistant transcript 19 Sep; GXP deck.   |   Case study 02/10

We first heard from Kate, our MO proxy stakeholder, about the promise created by preference questions and the operational burden of fulfilment. Further MO conversations helped us understand agent-mediated booking and the staffing constraints around high-touch service.

Our final research record reports five short conversations with guests matching our chosen profile at Hong Kong MO on 12 September; four said an assistant booked their stay. It also summarises three personal-agent interviews. These were small, accessible samples rather than representative research.

The Shenzhen MO visit introduced us to the Dream Maker role: a person who notices contextual signals and turns them into acts of care. This observation expanded the work beyond collecting information before arrival.

One executive assistant described familiar telephone coordination as effective. She was wary of putting private needs into another platform and wanted an accountable manager to acknowledge requests. She was more positive about optional menus, visible room differences and clear prices. We treat this as early concept feedback, not a test of the completed prototype.
The newly reviewed transcript is not counted as an additional fourth agent: its relationship to the three-agent summary is unverified.
An interview-reported estimate of agent booking within the selected segment; no underlying dataset supplied.
A local guest sample supporting the relevance of assistants; no population estimate.
Paraphrased findings in the final deck; the full recruitment and sampling record is incomplete.
A team-coded review sample concerning situational services; neither a hotel complaint rate nor an outcome measure.
Who we could not adequately reach

We did not secure a broad sample of staying guests, the full chain of procurement and travel intermediaries, or property teams across shifts and departments. We had no real post-design user testing with agents or hotel staff. We also lacked operational logs, approved cost data and a verified return-rate baseline.

The supplied GXP material provides an important organisational countercheck: MO already describes preference records, traces, task delegation and service guidance. We therefore position our work as a proposed extension to an existing service system.
We moved from collecting more preferences to making selected needs easier to express, interpret and fulfil. The four lines below are our evidence-qualified synthesis.
Sources: process node 683:2; Kate interviews; 19 Sep assistant transcript; supplied GXP material.   |   Case study 03/10
We believed that collecting guests’ expressed preferences before arrival would allow the hotel to prepare a room that felt like home from the moment they entered.

The evidence shows that assistants often mediate bookings in our selected context, while some needs emerge only during the stay. It also shows that trusted calls can already work well, some private needs are deliberately withheld, and MO already has preference records and service guidance.

So we now believe that helping these guests feel recognised depends on connecting the needs they choose to share with trusted human judgement and a feasible service response. Optional visual prompts may help assistants express unfamiliar possibilities; Dream Makers may add contextual understanding, provided each action has consent, ownership and delivery limits.

We would be wrong if existing trusted channels already conveyed the relevant needs adequately, if target assistants preferred those channels to our prototype, or if the added discovery and coordination failed to improve recognition within the hotel’s capacity.

Our workshop statement connected guest, agent and staff knowledge around the idea of “feeling at home”. The final playback sharpened this into two gaps: needs left unsaid online and situational observations that were difficult to share.

On reviewing the full assistant transcript and GXP deck, we had to qualify that story. More disclosure is not always desirable, and a lack of disclosure is not automatically a failure of texting. We cannot claim that MO has no shared process. Our proposed contribution is a clearer connection between optional expression, situational learning and operational confirmation.
What the service has to connect
What can be shared for this stay, through a channel the guest and assistant trust?
What is wanted, unwanted, uncertain or deliberately private?
What is a useful clue, and what still requires clarification?
Who can deliver, by when, at what cost, and who confirms it?
Fig. 2. A reading of the service relationship, redrawn for this case study. These are questions for validation, not confirmed user behaviours.
What we chose, and what we set aside
18 September–early October. We developed two connected touchpoints rather than expanding the preference questionnaire indefinitely.
Sources: process pages; app explorations; final presentation; 5 Oct project-context record; 19 Sep assistant transcript.   |   Case study 04/10
We chose an assistant-facing visual flow

We used the purpose of the stay to surface potentially relevant room and service choices. A visual room offered a concrete way to discuss arrangements that an assistant might not otherwise think to request. We kept a review step so that a selected option could be checked before submission.

We treated purpose as a starting point rather than a complete description of a guest. The assistant interview challenged our early business-versus-leisure generalisation: familiarity with the guest and the service relationship can matter more than trip category.
We chose a Dream Maker coordination layer

We paired online preparation with in-person discovery. The Dream Maker workspace structures a possible act of care into a plan, approval, departmental feasibility check, execution and review. It is intended to make learning reusable without removing individual judgement.

This adds a proposed workflow around situational care. It does not establish that MO needs its first preference database or its first SOP. The supplied GXP framework already includes profile information, traces and minimum service guidance.
We set aside an all-guest, all-property solution. The focused segment and urban context made the design more manageable, but limit how widely our conclusions can travel.
We did not pursue exhaustive mandatory questions or interaction for its own sake. Skipping, saying “not needed” and keeping a trusted human channel remain necessary design conditions.
We did not propose replacing the hotel’s core property system. Any production version would need an agreed connection to existing records and task handling. That integration is unresolved.

We also rejected automatic promises of bespoke service. Suggested plans must remain provisional until the relevant people confirm capacity, cost and timing. A declined or revised plan needs a visible explanation.
Fig. 3. Stay-purpose / preference-area matrix in the process file, named 5 October. We used purpose as a starting hypothesis, not a complete description of a guest.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   05  SERVICE / AS-IS
The service as we understood it
We assembled the current journey from interviews, site visits and the supplied GXP “Today” workflow. It is a composite account, not an audited process for every MO property.
Sources: GXP slides 2, 6, 24–31; interviews; stakeholder map and blueprint in the process file.   |   Case study 05/10
Assistant arranges the stay; other intermediaries may be involved.
Reservations or an established relationship contact receives the brief.
Match profiles, review tier/VIP status, record purpose and preferences.
Our three-role model simplifies corporate procurement, travel platforms and local hosts.
Guest or assistant chooses what to share and how.
Property outreach; Guest Relations / Front Office follows up in a preferred channel.
Review arrivals at 14, 7 and 3 days; delegate traces and service preparation.
No live logs showing response time, handoff loss or the prevalence of rework.
Guest encounters the prepared room and service.
Welcome, check-in and contextual conversation; Dream Maker care where observed.
Coordinate room readiness, amenities and departmental actions.
The Dream Maker observation came from Shenzhen; the role cannot be assumed identical elsewhere.
Guest requests, accepts or declines further care.
Staff respond and may notice new preferences.
Update relevant records, follow up and confirm tasks.
We did not observe every department, shift or complete request-to-delivery cycle.
Fig. 4. Composite As-Is journey. The supplied GXP deck distinguishes its existing “Today” process from a proposed “Tomorrow with GXP” process; we keep that distinction.

MO’s material distinguishes declared, observed and directly stated preferences, reservation notes and actionable traces. It also describes minimum guidance and service tempo. Our earlier “no standard SOP” wording was too broad and is withdrawn.

We could not verify a universal absence of coordination. We instead explored whether selected assistants need a clearer way to express possibilities, and whether situational Dream Maker learning can be linked more explicitly to feasible, owned actions within the existing framework.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   05  SERVICE / TO-BE
We proposed a connection from optional expression to an accountable response. A request, an observation, a proposed plan and a confirmed arrangement must remain different states.
Sources: final blueprint; Dream Maker workflow and prototype; app prototype; GXP programme material.   |   Case study 06/10
The assistant explores relevant room options, skips what is unnecessary and reviews the brief.
Reservations links explicit requests to the correct stay and records who supplied them.
Viewing an option does not create a request. Submission is not fulfilment.
A named contact acknowledges the brief and asks only for missing essentials.
Guest Relations / Front Office checks authority, timing, privacy and existing preferences.
Unknown information stays unknown; no inferred preference becomes a fact.
The Dream Maker notices a possible act of care and clarifies where needed.
Draft the plan; identify resources, cost and timing; obtain appropriate supervisory approval.
An observation is a clue. A plan is provisional until feasibility is confirmed.
The contact confirms a deliverable arrangement or explains an alternative.
Departments confirm resources and accept tasks; material changes return for review.
Each action needs an owner, deadline and status. No confirmation while resources are pending.
The guest receives the service, declines it or requests a change.
Teams record delivery; the Dream Maker captures response and a reusable case, subject to policy.
Record what happened, including rejection and failure; distinguish evidence from interpretation.
Fig. 5. Proposed To-Be service sequence. Ownership and system connections are recommendations; MO has not approved or implemented them through this project.

The online touchpoint prepares a more legible starting brief. The offline touchpoint supports contextual care and cross-department coordination. We retain a human relationship around both, including acknowledgement, clarification and the option to use an existing channel.
What remains to be worked out

The prototype does not connect to live availability, guest records, budgets or task systems. Permissions, retention, assistant authority, late bookings and room changes still require property-level agreement and operational testing.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   05  SERVICE / PROTOTYPES
By early October, our work had become an assistant-facing room flow and a Dream Maker workspace. Both demonstrate interactions; neither proves live service performance.
Sources: MO App Prototype / Business Demo; MO Dream Maker prototype; 5 Oct context record; final presentation.   |   Case study 07/10

We organised choices around the stay’s purpose, then room zones and service details. The later mobile flow lets an assistant inspect the room, set relevant preferences and review the stay brief. These choices make possible arrangements visible; they do not replace the conversation with a trusted contact.
Begin with your desk essentials, then add the equipment and support you need for your business day.
Writing essentials at your desk, ready when you are.
A focused reading light at your desk.
A universal adapter and charging cable for your devices.
Add a screen and an HDMI cable for your own work.
Request copies of the documents you need for your work.
Let us prepare the essentials, so you can settle into your work.
Review your room and the details we will prepare.
Harbour Room · Level 2 · Up to 6 guests
Your room preferences will guide preparation for this visit.
Fig. 6. Work-area preferences and review screens, cloned as editable frames from our final mobile prototype.

Our earlier web prototype explored bed-side selection, temperature and spatial comments. It separated exploration from explicit selection. We still need to test whether the later flow makes skipping, “not needed” and uncertainty clear.

We structured discovery into a proposed plan, supervisory review, resource confirmation, task coordination and outcome review. Suggestions remain aids to human judgement. The workspace represents a possible operational layer, with mock content and no verified system integration.
Guest Workspace / Mr. Wang / Service Plan
Mr. Wang · Current draft; not yet submitted for approval.
Provide Mr. Wang with flexible cultural recommendations.

Resources · Concierge information check / 1 recommendation card
Timing · Agree after confirming interest; minimise disturbance
Confirm feasibility, clear ownership and estimated resources.
The demo is already up to date
Fig. 7. A service-plan draft in the Dream Maker prototype. It supports planning; it is not evidence that a hotel team accepted or delivered the plan.

We used simple simulated walkthroughs to explore how the interfaces and sequence might work. We did not run real post-design tests with assistants, guests or hotel staff, and did not test the service in a live property. The prototype therefore supports a proposition, not a claim of faster booking, lower workload or increased loyalty.
28 September–2 October. Building the tracker exposed a gap between attractive targets and numbers we could actually defend. We preserve that distinction here.
Sources: Class 9 tracker / node 732:2; Class 10 / node 812:2; final expected-outcomes page; interview notes.   |   Case study 08/10
Time to communicate an agreed request, plus accuracy. “>5 min” is interview self-report; 3 min was our target.
Total staff minutes per usable, confirmed request, including clarification and rework.
Skip / decline use, misunderstandings and privacy concerns during a task.
Share of accepted requests that are feasible, confirmed and delivered as agreed.
Guest or assistant can identify what is confirmed and who to contact.
Task ownership coverage, missed deadlines and unresolved changes.
Guest response to the delivered care, including unwanted or intrusive service.
Cost to serve and service-recovery incidents; loyalty as a later, separate outcome.
Table 1. A proposed measurement plan reconstructed from the tracker. These role owners have not accepted responsibility through the project.
Claims we cannot carry forward as results

The final deck’s 89.5% → 97.5% capture-rate claim transferred general survey item-nonresponse findings into hotel performance. That inference is unsupported. The review sample’s 11 → 0 complaint target and a 15–25% retention uplift are also untested assumptions, not observed improvements.

We would agree one request definition, start/stop timestamps and a complete workload boundary before a pilot. We would compare the same task through the existing channel and prototype, then track fulfilment separately. Owners must agree baselines, thresholds and reporting cadence before any success claim.
What would have proved us wrong
2 October onward. We wrote failure conditions, but our validation remained a simple simulation. The strongest corrections came from evidence that challenged the framing and the numbers.
Sources: Class 10 criteria / node 812:2; assistant transcript 19 Sep; GXP deck; team confirmation of simulation-only testing.   |   Case study 09/10
What actually broke in our reasoning

Our broad claim that texting prevents needs from being shared did not survive the full assistant account. Trusted telephone coordination could already be efficient, while some information was deliberately withheld. A new interface could add effort or reduce trust instead of helping.

Our “no standard SOP” claim also exceeded the evidence. MO’s supplied material already specifies a preference-to-action framework and minimum guidance. We had to narrow the contribution to a proposed assistant expression flow and a more explicit situational-care coordination layer.

The numerical outcome story broke at the evidence boundary. Survey nonresponse, a small review sample and assumed retention uplift could not establish hotel performance. The case therefore reports these as withdrawn claims or untested targets.
What our simulation did not establish

We did not conduct real post-design user tests or observe live service delivery. We have no reliable task-by-task measurements of time saved, misunderstandings, staff effort or fulfilment failures. Functional interaction checks and a team walkthrough cannot establish desirability or operational feasibility.
The conditions under which we would stop
We would stop or redesign if target assistants preferred the existing channel, refused the interactive flow, or felt it exposed information they did not want recorded.
We would stop or reduce scope if the flow failed to produce usable, confirmed requests, or raised total staff effort beyond an agreed capacity and cost limit.
We would reject the service claim if more information was collected but arrangements were not delivered as agreed, or the resulting care felt unwanted or failed to improve recognition.
How we would test those conditions next

We would ask real assistants to complete the same request through the existing channel and prototype, then ask property staff to simulate the complete handoff. We would record errors, omitted needs, clarification, total effort and delivery decisions. The hotel and research team must agree failure thresholds before the session.
Our original Class 10 sheet also tied success to return rate. We now treat loyalty as a later hypothesis: an unchanged return rate alone would not identify which part of the service failed.
The course ended with a service proposition and prototypes. The next step is a property-owned validation effort, with a narrow scope and explicit delivery boundaries.
Sources: assigned brief; staffing constraints in MO interviews; final risks page; proposed follow-up plan in this case study.   |   Case study 10/10

We would begin with one property, one defined guest group and a small set of deliverable room and service requests. We would map the proposal onto the property’s current GXP, profile and trace processes, and identify where it adds value rather than duplicates work.

Before any real guest use, the hotel would need to agree who may act for a guest, what information may be recorded, what requires consent, how long it is retained and who may see it. A human contact must remain available, and guests and assistants must be able to decline the digital route.

We would establish the existing-channel baseline, run comparative assistant tasks and carry out a staff simulation across departments. Late booking, changed room, declined service, unavailable resources and a revised plan should all be included.

Only after those tasks meet agreed criteria would we propose a limited live pilot. We would monitor confirmed-request quality, delivery reliability, total staff effort and guest response. Wider rollout and claims about loyalty or spend would require further evidence.
Who would need to own the work
Approve scope, staffing capacity, budget and the decision to proceed or stop.
Own the guest-facing promise and the cross-department service journey.
Own assistant intake, acknowledgement, clarification and the request-quality baseline.
Accept tasks and confirm resources, timing, delivery and exceptions.
Agree access, integration with existing systems, security and retention.
Agree cost-to-serve measures and the balance between service value and operational load.
These are proposed roles, not appointments or commitments obtained during the course.
What we can hand over now

We can hand over the research trail, the reframed brief, the two prototypes, a proposed journey and workflow, the revised tracker and explicit failure conditions. We cannot hand over an approved operating model or demonstrated business outcome. That is the boundary between our completed course work and the work still to be agreed.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A01
The first wall: what we knew and assumed
We began by separating the brief’s claims from our own assumptions and the questions that required evidence. The photographs preserve that early uncertainty.
Sources: project archive wall photographs 01 and 04. Workshop sequence supported by S02–S03 course materials.   |   Appendix A01/10
Fig. A1. Facts / Assumptions / What we need to check. Original wall photograph.

The exercise forced us to distinguish what the assigned brief had already stated from what we still needed to learn. Operational complexity was given in the brief. Guest motivations, preferred channels and what “feeling at home” meant were still open questions.
The wall is evidence of our framing process. It is not independent evidence that the assumptions written on its notes were true.
Fig. A2. Who is named / who is missing, and our early intent. Original wall photograph.
From a guest-only frame to a service relationship

We began with the staying guest, then examined the assistant and the hotel teams who translate and deliver the request. This helped us see why the person using a booking interface might not be the person who experiences the room.
The later assistant interview broadened the chain again: procurement, travel platforms, local hosts and trusted account contacts may also intervene. Our simplified map remains a design model.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A02
We keep dated source records separate from later synthesis. An interview report, a field observation and a measured service outcome carry different kinds of weight.
Source register: supplied Drive course folder; project transcripts and context in iCloud; original Figma research and final presentation.   |   Appendix A02/10
Expectation management, operational complexity, cost to serve and the commercial intent after booking.
An audited NPS model, quantified process baseline or verified current operating performance.
Context for the halted personalisation effort and the tension between recognition and fulfilment.
A full failure report or direct testimony from all affected departments.
Five guest conversations reported in the research summary.
Four of five said an assistant arranged their booking; this supported our chosen focus.
A representative share of guests or independent verification of wealth or VIP status.
Further MO interview and meeting summary.
Agent involvement, high-touch service context and operational constraints.
The raw booking dataset behind the reported 95% estimate.
Trusted-channel counterexample; privacy concerns; optional menus, visible choices and manager acknowledgement.
Behaviour on the final prototype. Identity linkage to the three-agent summary is not confirmed.
Shenzhen visit, three-agent synthesis and 16-review coding in the final deck.
Dream Maker discovery; selected accounts of coordination and situational service.
Uniform practice across properties, a complaint rate or a service improvement.
Existing preference taxonomy, Today workflow, traces, minimum guidance and a proposed Tomorrow workflow.
Verified rollout status, the stopped pilot’s failure analysis, or live property compliance.
Working migration summary and room-prototype archive.
Evolution of the spatial interface and issues still open at that date.
Final approved requirements, user-test results or live system integration.
We use anonymised research summaries. We omit private third-party details that are irrelevant to the service-design question.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A03
How the research changed our scope
The process did not move directly from one problem to one interface. We repeatedly adjusted who the service was for and what kind of knowledge it needed.
Sources: early walls; process conclusion / node 683:2; 19 Sep assistant transcript; Shenzhen visit synthesis; 5 Oct working context.   |   Appendix A03/10
We began with the belief that knowing preferences before arrival would help prepare a room that felt like home. That position made preference collection appear to be the central design problem.

The guest and agent research shifted our attention towards the person representing the staying guest. An assistant might know routines and schedules but still need to recognise which hotel arrangements were possible. This gave us a reason to explore visible, concrete choices rather than only an empty text field.
The second shift: care in context

At Shenzhen MO, the Dream Maker role suggested that relevant needs could emerge in a conversation or situation that a pre-arrival form could never fully predict. We widened the service from a collection interface to a relationship between preparation, observation and response.

Our original four-line workshop statement therefore connected guest, agent and staff knowledge and asked what “feeling at home” meant to each guest. The shared guest profile and handoff process became part of the concept, alongside the online touchpoint.
The challenge inside our own evidence

The 19 September assistant transcript prevents a simple “phones and texts are inefficient” conclusion. Familiarity made requests easier; a trusted manager mattered; privacy could make less disclosure the right outcome. We therefore treat visual expression as an option for a specific need, not a universal replacement channel.

The supplied GXP deck also prevents an “MO has no process” conclusion. It documents existing information categories and traces. This case study now describes our proposal as building on that foundation and gives the narrower claims explicit limits.
Help the assistant recognise and communicate selected possibilities; acknowledge the request.
Allow contextual discovery, with clarification and respect for privacy.
Translate a chosen response into a feasible plan with an owner and a visible status.
Keep outcomes and rejected assumptions available for learning, subject to policy.
This is a retrospective account of the reasoning. It does not imply that every qualification was resolved in the final presentation.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A04
App audit and early room explorations
We examined the existing digital experience and explored a spatial interface. The archive shows interaction possibilities, rather than evidence that these interactions improved a user’s task.
Sources: original App audit / node 345:21; room exploration images 874:108 and 879:115; 5 Oct context and archived prototype source.   |   Appendix A04/10

The existing app capture already shows concrete choices, including a late-checkout time selection. Our work was therefore not the invention of selectable preferences. We explored how room context and stay purpose might help an assistant identify additional relevant arrangements.
Fig. A3. Existing MO app capture from our audit: late-checkout options. This is research reference material, not our redesigned screen.
The audit alone did not show that guests misunderstood this screen, or that a spatial interface would perform better. That comparison still requires task-based research.
We explored direct interaction with the room
Fig. A4. Early spatial prototype: room hotspots, temperature and preferred bed side.
Fig. A5. A later state in the exploration: comments anchored to a location in the room.

We moved editing into the illustration rather than a fixed side panel. We then added bed-side dragging, a temperature wheel and comment editing. Viewed, explicitly selected and not specified were distinct states; exploring a feature did not itself create a service request.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A05
From a stakeholder wall to an information map
We mapped who knows something about the guest, who passes it on and who delivers the service. Drawing a connection did not verify that the handoff worked.
Sources: Outcomes / StakeholderMap.jpg; digitised workshop map in process node 734:4; final stakeholder synthesis.   |   Appendix A05/10
Fig. A6. Original workshop stakeholder map. The photograph preserves the work as it stood.
What the wall helped us see

The map put the assistant outside the hotel but inside the service relationship. Reservations, welcome staff, the front desk, Dream Maker and service departments could each hold a different part of the guest’s context.
This made the handoff itself a design concern. A preference needed both a route into the hotel and a route to the people able to act on it.
Fig. A7. Existing digitisation of the workshop map. Dashed links preserve uncertainty in the photographed drawing.
What the map still leaves out
The simplified model does not represent every procurement route, travel intermediary, authority boundary or system permission. We did not verify each arrow through real operational records.
The later proposal adds clearer ownership and confirmation states. Those additions are design decisions to be tested, not discoveries already established by this diagram.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A06
The blueprint as a working artefact
We used the journey to connect the visible guest experience with preparation and coordination behind it. The workshop sheet mixed current activity with ideas we wanted to try.
Sources: Outcomes / ServiceBlueprint.jpg; digitised workshop journey in node 734:3; final blueprints and process notes.   |   Appendix A06/10
Fig. A8. Original service-blueprint photograph. Handwritten additions show the work developing.
From booking to the first room encounter

We followed the guest from discussing travel with an assistant through booking, preparation, pickup, check-in and room entry. The lower rows made preparation, preference records and departmental coordination visible.
This expanded the problem beyond the booking interface: a clear brief is useful only if the hotel can interpret it and deliver the arrangement.
Fig. A9. Existing digitisation of the workshop journey. It separates overlaid concept notes and marks obscured text.
Why the final case separates As-Is and To-Be
The workshop artefact contains proposed playful interactions alongside descriptions of current work. Treating the entire sheet as an observed process would overstate the evidence.

Pages 05–06 therefore distinguish a composite current journey, grounded partly in GXP’s Today workflow, from our proposed service. Neither diagram establishes that every MO property operates identically.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A07
Storyboard and the limits of simulation
We used a storyboard to make the proposed service sequence concrete. Its ending is an intended experience, not an observed guest outcome.
Sources: Outcomes / StoryBoard.png; original storyboard node 734:2; team confirmation that post-design testing was a simple simulation.   |   Appendix A07/10
Fig. A10. Our six-scene pre-arrival storyboard. Original illustration; undated in the supplied archive.
What we tried to make explicit
A conversation establishes travel intent and known routines; the assistant may contribute additional context.
Visible options could make possible arrangements easier to recognise and express.
The assistant can communicate a useful brief without excessive effort.
The hotel distinguishes what can and cannot be arranged before the assistant reports back.
A Dream Maker may notice something the pre-arrival brief did not contain. The original scene leaves the method “TBD”.
The guest feels appropriately recognised by the preparation and care received. This was the desired ending.
What we can say about the walkthrough

We had only a simple simulated test of the design. We did not recruit real assistants or hotel staff to complete the final service tasks. The archive does not supply a reliable task-level record of timings, misunderstandings or actions that could not be executed.

The storyboard makes assumptions visible: the assistant will engage, a request will reach a decision-maker, arrival contact will be available and the hotel can fulfil the plan. It does not show that those assumptions held.

For a next test we would include refusal, no additional need, unavailable capacity and a late change, then record both the user experience and the complete staff workload. This is a proposed test, not one already conducted.
THE UNSAID   /   MANDARIN ORIENTAL   /   09  APPENDIX / A08
The assistant prototype evolved through several forms
By 5 October, we had documented a working spatial prototype. The later Figma flow expanded the concept into a mobile stay-planning journey.
Sources: SD5412_PROJECT_CONTEXT.md dated 5 Oct; archived mo-room-prototype / dist; process capture 992:368; final app Business Demo.   |   Appendix A08/10
What changed in the working record
A room plan on the left, fixed editing and summary panel on the right, and simulated submission.
Editing moved into room popovers; comments could be anchored to a chosen location.
English interface; bed-side drag and snap; a vertical temperature wheel; comment add, edit and delete.

A distinction we wanted to preserve

We began with a tension in luxury hospitality: asking about a preference creates an expectation. More questions can multiply combinations of room preparation, timing and service requests, while staff capacity, room changes and cost to serve remain constrained. The brief described an earlier hyper-personalisation pilot that had been stopped because of operational complexity.

We were asked to build engagement and manage expectations after booking and before arrival, without over-promising. The commercial intent was brand equity, loyalty and spending on property. This was not a booking-conversion brief.
The brief as we reframed it

We are solving for pre-arrival care that helps guests feel recognised and can be delivered reliably at manageable cost and complexity, in service of Mandarin Oriental’s goal of strengthening brand equity and guests’ willingness to pay.

We chose an urban MO context and a high-net-worth guest segment, often represented by a human assistant. The “top 5%” boundary was our design focus, not a verified segment size. We connected what the assistant knows before arrival with what a Dream Maker may notice in person, then asked how both could become an owned, feasible service response.

Sources: process node 683:2; Kate interviews; 19 Sep assistant transcript; supplied GXP material.   |   Case study 03/10
We believed that collecting guests’ expressed preferences before arrival would allow the hotel to prepare a room that felt like home from the moment they entered.

The evidence shows that assistants often mediate bookings in our selected context, while some needs emerge only during the stay. It also shows that trusted calls can already work well, some private needs are deliberately withheld, and MO already has preference records and service guidance.

So we now believe that helping these guests feel recognised depends on connecting the needs they choose to share with trusted human judgement and a feasible service response. Optional visual prompts may help assistants express unfamiliar possibilities; Dream Makers may add contextual understanding, provided each action has consent, ownership and delivery limits.

We would be wrong if existing trusted channels already conveyed the relevant needs adequately, if target assistants preferred those channels to our prototype, or if the added discovery and coordination failed to improve recognition within the hotel’s capacity.

Our workshop statement connected guest, agent and staff knowledge around the idea of “feeling at home”. The final playback sharpened this into two gaps: needs left unsaid online and situational observations that were difficult to share.

On reviewing the full assistant transcript and GXP deck, we had to qualify that story. More disclosure is not always desirable, and a lack of disclosure is not automatically a failure of texting. We cannot claim that MO has no shared process. Our proposed contribution is a clearer connection between optional expression, situational learning and operational confirmation.

Claims we cannot carry forward as results

The final deck’s 89.5% → 97.5% capture-rate claim transferred general survey item-nonresponse findings into hotel performance. That inference is unsupported. The review sample’s 11 → 0 complaint target and a 15–25% retention uplift are also untested assumptions, not observed improvements.

We would agree one request definition, start/stop timestamps and a complete workload boundary before a pilot. We would compare the same task through the existing channel and prototype, then track fulfilment separately. Owners must agree baselines, thresholds and reporting cadence before any success claim.
What would have proved us wrong
2 October onward. We wrote failure conditions, but our validation remained a simple simulation. The strongest corrections came from evidence that challenged the framing and the numbers.
Sources: Class 10 criteria / node 812:2; assistant transcript 19 Sep; GXP deck; team confirmation of simulation-only testing.   |   Case study 09/10
What actually broke in our reasoning

Our broad claim that texting prevents needs from being shared did not survive the full assistant account. Trusted telephone coordination could already be efficient, while some information was deliberately withheld. A new interface could add effort or reduce trust instead of helping.

Our “no standard SOP” claim also exceeded the evidence. MO’s supplied material already specifies a preference-to-action framework and minimum guidance. We had to narrow the contribution to a proposed assistant expression flow and a more explicit situational-care coordination layer.

The numerical outcome story broke at the evidence boundary. Survey nonresponse, a small review sample and assumed retention uplift could not establish hotel performance. The case therefore reports these as withdrawn claims or untested targets.
What our simulation did not establish

We did not conduct real post-design user tests or observe live service delivery. We have no reliable task-by-task measurements of time saved, misunderstandings, staff effort or fulfilment failures. Functional interaction checks and a team walkthrough cannot establish desirability or operational feasibility.
The conditions under which we would stop
We would stop or redesign if target assistants preferred the existing channel, refused the interactive flow, or felt it exposed information they did not want recorded.
We would stop or reduce scope if the flow failed to produce usable, confirmed requests, or raised total staff effort beyond an agreed capacity and cost limit.
We would reject the service claim if more information was collected but arrangements were not delivered as agreed, or the resulting care felt unwanted or failed to improve recognition.
How we would test those conditions next

We would ask real assistants to complete the same request through the existing channel and prototype, then ask property staff to simulate the complete handoff. We would record errors, omitted needs, clarification, total effort and delivery decisions. The hotel and research team must agree failure thresholds before the session.
Our original Class 10 sheet also tied success to return rate. We now treat loyalty as a later hypothesis: an unchanged return rate alone would not identify which part of the service failed.
The course ended with a service proposition and prototypes. The next step is a property-owned validation effort, with a narrow scope and explicit delivery boundaries.
Sources: assigned brief; staffing constraints in MO interviews; final risks page; proposed follow-up plan in this case study.   |   Case study 10/10

We would begin with one property, one defined guest group and a small set of deliverable room and service requests. We would map the proposal onto the property’s current GXP, profile and trace processes, and identify where it adds value rather than duplicates work.

Before any real guest use, the hotel would need to agree who may act for a guest, what information may be recorded, what requires consent, how long it is retained and who may see it. A human contact must remain available, and guests and assistants must be able to decline the digital route.

We would establish the existing-channel baseline, run comparative assistant tasks and carry out a staff simulation across departments. Late booking, changed room, declined service, unavailable resources and a revised plan should all be included.

Only after those tasks meet agreed criteria would we propose a limited live pilot. We would monitor confirmed-request quality, delivery reliability, total staff effort and guest response. Wider rollout and claims about loyalty or spend would require further evidence.

What the wall helped us see

The map put the assistant outside the hotel but inside the service relationship. Reservations, welcome staff, the front desk, Dream Maker and service departments could each hold a different part of the guest’s context.
This made the handoff itself a design concern. A preference needed both a route into the hotel and a route to the people able to act on it.

What the map still leaves out
The simplified model does not represent every procurement route, travel intermediary, authority boundary or system permission. We did not verify each arrow through real operational records.
The later proposal adds clearer ownership and confirmation states. Those additions are design decisions to be tested, not discoveries already established by this diagram.

Storyboard and the limits of simulation
We used a storyboard to make the proposed service sequence concrete. Its ending is an intended experience, not an observed guest outcome.
Sources: Outcomes / StoryBoard.png; original storyboard node 734:2; team confirmation that post-design testing was a simple simulation.   |   Appendix A07/10
Fig. A10. Our six-scene pre-arrival storyboard. Original illustration; undated in the supplied archive.
What we tried to make explicit
A conversation establishes travel intent and known routines; the assistant may contribute additional context.
Visible options could make possible arrangements easier to recognise and express.
The assistant can communicate a useful brief without excessive effort.
The hotel distinguishes what can and cannot be arranged before the assistant reports back.
A Dream Maker may notice something the pre-arrival brief did not contain. The original scene leaves the method “TBD”.
The guest feels appropriately recognised by the preparation and care received. This was the desired ending.
What we can say about the walkthrough

We had only a simple simulated test of the design. We did not recruit real assistants or hotel staff to complete the final service tasks. The archive does not supply a reliable task-level record of timings, misunderstandings or actions that could not be executed.

The storyboard makes assumptions visible: the assistant will engage, a request will reach a decision-maker, arrival contact will be available and the hotel can fulfil the plan. It does not show that those assumptions held.

For a next test we would include refusal, no additional need, unavailable capacity and a late change, then record both the user experience and the complete staff workload. This is a proposed test, not one already conducted.
